newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government urged to review immigration laws.
newsitem.headline: French government urged to review immigration laws.

text.p: France's Human Rights Commission on Friday urged the government to review the country's tough immigration laws, which have drawn wide criticism at home and abroad.
The government-appointed watchdog said it "strongly requests the whole array of legal provisions regarding foreigners be sent back to the drawing board".

It said laws passed in 1993 to radically curb immigration "gave rise to very serious distortions leading to situations contrary to human dignity without really solving illegal immigration and clandestine labour".
The commission, whose opinions are not binding, was commenting on a bill approved by the cabinet last week to remove anomalies created by the 1993 laws.
The bill, which must go before parliament, would boost police powers to crack down on illegal immigration while making it easier for some families to obtain residence permits.

It aims to plug legal loopholes that have embarrassed the government particularly after police stormed a church and evicted 210 African immigrants in August. Ten of the immigrants were on a hunger strike in protest of their uncertain status.
The commission said it had "most serious reservations" about the new bill.

It said that although the bill would clear up the status of a number of immigrants, it could threaten individual freedom and institute a special criminal law for foreigners in breach of the basic principle of equal justice for all.

Left-wing parties and human rights groups have repeatedly urged the centre-right government to review or repeal the 1993 laws, which they say were a sap to Jean-Marie Le Pen's far-right National Front party which advocates sending millions of immigrants home.

Some immigrants have successfully fought expulsion under the laws, named after former interior minister Charles Pasqua, by arguing that they violated a European convention guaranteeing family integrity.
The 1993 laws have also come under attack abroad -- United Nations' investigator Maurice Glele-Ahanhanzo has said France was being shaken by "a wave of xenophobia and racism".
He said in a report to the U.N. Human Rights Commission earlier this year that the laws had worsened problems faced by foreigners in France and he recommended that they be amended.
